records.source: אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֧ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־יִרְמְיָ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא עַל־הַגּוֹיִֽם׃
records.gloss: [That] which came, [the] word of Yahweh, to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.
pieces: This message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to the prophet Jeremiah about the nations:

L.1: That which came [as] the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations:

R.1: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jeremiah the prophet about the nations:

decisions.choice: the oracles against the nations begin here, as the Hebrew text orders the book
decisions.reason: This heading opens the oracles against the nations (chapters 46-51): Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, Elam, and last Babylon. The Greek translation of Jeremiah places these oracles after 25:13 and in a different order; see the note at 1:1. The Hebrew order is followed here. This is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: a heading: "what came as the word of the LORD"
decisions.reason: The verse opens with "which", the same unusual form of heading as 14:1, 47:1 and 49:34. It names what follows as the word of the LORD to Jeremiah, here a word about the nations rather than about Judah (compare 1:5, 10, where Jeremiah is appointed a prophet to the nations).

decisions.choice: That which came [as] the word of the LORD ... / This message from the LORD came to the prophet Jeremiah ... / This is the message the LORD gave Jeremiah ...
decisions.reason: The heading is worded as 14:1, which has the same Hebrew form; Balanced and Readable say "message" as the book's settled heading formulas do ("This message came to Jeremiah from the LORD"), and Balanced makes the heading a sentence.

records.heading: Egypt's army at Carchemish

records.source: לְמִצְרַ֗יִם עַל־חֵ֨יל פַּרְעֹ֤ה נְכוֹ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁר־הָיָ֥ה עַל־נְהַר־פְּרָ֖ת בְּכַרְכְּמִ֑שׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִכָּ֗ה נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל בִּשְׁנַת֙ הָֽרְבִיעִ֔ית לִיהוֹיָקִ֥ים בֶּן־יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: Concerning Egypt: concerning [the] army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, which was by [the] river Euphrates at Carchemish, which defeated Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon in the year the fourth of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah.
pieces: About Egypt. About the army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, camped by the Euphrates River at Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:

L.2: Concerning Egypt: concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:

R.2: This message is about Egypt. It is about the army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt. His army was camped by the Euphrates River at the city of Carchemish. Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated it in Jehoiakim's fourth year as king of Judah. Jehoiakim was Josiah's son.

decisions.choice: the battle of Carchemish, 605 BC
decisions.reason: Pharaoh Neco (Neco II) had marched north to the Euphrates in 609 BC, killing Josiah on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Carchemish, a fortress city on the upper Euphrates, was his base. Jehoiakim became king in 609 BC, so his fourth year was 605 BC, the year Nebuchadrezzar crushed the Egyptian army there and became king of Babylon (25:1; 36:1). After it Egypt lost all its land between the Wadi of Egypt and the Euphrates (2 Kings 24:7).

decisions.choice: which was ... which defeated: both clauses describe the army
decisions.reason: The first "which" places the army at Carchemish; the second says it was the army Nebuchadrezzar defeated. The heading dates the poem of verses 3-12 to that battle.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the form of the name with r, as the Hebrew has it here
decisions.reason: As at 25:1, the Hebrew spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar, closer to the Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur. Elsewhere it is Nebuchadnezzar; both name the same king.

decisions.choice: the river Euphrates (Literal); the Euphrates River (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew names the river here ("the river Perath"), so it is not the bare "the River" of other verses. The wording follows 2 Kings 23:29 and 24:7, which tell of the same Pharaoh and the same river.

decisions.choice: This message is about ... His army was camped ... the city of
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the heading into sentences and supplies "camped" (as Balanced does) and "the city of" to make plain that the army was stationed at a city by the river. The date follows the wording set for dated headings in Jeremiah: "the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim" (Balanced), "Jehoiakim's fourth year as king" (Readable).

records.source: עִרְכ֤וּ מָגֵן֙ וְצִנָּ֔ה וּגְשׁ֖וּ לַמִּלְחָמָֽה׃
records.gloss: Set in order buckler and shield, and draw near to the battle.
pieces: Make ready the small shield and the large, \q and advance into battle!

L.3: Set in order buckler and shield, \q and draw near for battle!

R.3: Get your shields ready, small and large! \q March out to fight!

decisions.choice: buckler and shield: the small round shield and the large body shield
decisions.reason: The first word is the light round shield carried by a soldier in hand-to-hand fighting; the second is the large shield that covered the whole body (1 Kings 10:16-17). Together they mean the whole army, light troops and heavy, getting ready.

decisions.choice: the commands are spoken to Egypt's army, and are soon mocked
decisions.reason: The poem opens with the orders of a commander calling his troops to battle (verses 3-4). Verse 5 shows the same army running in terror, so the orders sound bitterly ironic: all the preparation will come to nothing.

decisions.choice: the small shield and the large (Balanced); shields, small and large (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the two kinds of shield are (m1), since "buckler" is no longer a common word.

records.source: אִסְר֣וּ הַסּוּסִ֗ים וַֽעֲלוּ֙ הַפָּ֣רָשִׁ֔ים וְהִֽתְיַצְּב֖וּ בְּכ֥וֹבָעִ֑ים מִרְקוּ֙ הָֽרְמָחִ֔ים לִבְשׁ֖וּ הַסִּרְיֹנֹֽת׃
records.gloss: Harness the horses, and mount the steeds, and take your stand with helmets; polish the spears, put on the armor.
pieces: Harness the horses! Mount the warhorses! \q Take your positions with helmets on! \q Sharpen the spears, \q put on your coats of mail!

L.4: Harness the horses, and mount the steeds, \q and take your stand in helmets! \q Polish the spears, \q put on the armor!

R.4: Hitch up the horses! Get on your warhorses! \q Put on your helmets and stand in line! \q Sharpen your spears! \q Put on your armor!

decisions.choice: mount the steeds: get on the horses
decisions.reason: The second word can mean a horse used in war or the man who rides it. Beside "harness the horses" it most likely means the warhorses, so the order is to mount them. Read the other way, the line is "mount, you horsemen". The sense is much the same: the cavalry and chariots make ready.

decisions.choice: polish the spears: scour and sharpen them; the armor: coats of scale mail
decisions.reason: The verb means to scour or burnish metal, which also gives it a keen edge (compare Ezekiel 21:14-16, of a sword). The last word is the body armor of small metal plates worn by soldiers (1 Samuel 17:5; 1 Kings 22:34).

decisions.choice: sharpen; coats of mail (Balanced); armor (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "sharpen" because burnishing a spear also gave it its edge (m2); Balanced names the kind of armor, and Readable keeps the plain word.

records.source: מַדּ֣וּעַ רָאִ֗יתִי הֵ֣מָּה חַתִּים֮ נְסֹגִ֣ים אָחוֹר֒ וְגִבּוֹרֵיהֶ֣ם יֻכַּ֔תּוּ וּמָנ֥וֹס נָ֖סוּ וְלֹ֣א הִפְנ֑וּ מָג֥וֹר מִסָּבִ֖יב נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: Why have I seen? They [are] terrified, turning back, and their warriors are beaten down, and flight they have fled and not turned back; terror from all around, declares Yahweh.
pieces: Why do I see them panic-stricken, falling back? \q Their warriors are battered down; \q they run headlong and do not look back. \q Terror on every side! declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.5: Why have I seen them terrified, turning back? \q Their warriors are beaten down; \q they have fled in flight and do not look back. \q Terror on every side! declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.5: Why do I see them so afraid and running back? \q Their soldiers are beaten. \q They run away fast and do not look back. \q Terror all around! says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: why have I seen: the LORD sees the defeat as if it had already happened
decisions.reason: The speaker is the LORD ("declares the LORD"). He looks on the army that was just called to battle and sees it already broken and running. The verbs that follow are perfects, describing the rout as done.

decisions.choice: fled in flight: fled headlong
decisions.reason: The verb is joined to a noun from the same root, "they fled a flight", which stresses the running: they flee in a rout. They do not even turn to look behind them.

decisions.choice: terror on every side: one of Jeremiah's sayings
decisions.reason: The phrase is used in 6:25; 20:3, 10; 49:29 and Lamentations 2:22 (compare Psalm 31:14). Words first spoken of the enemy coming against Judah now fall on Egypt's army.

decisions.choice: Terror on every side (Literal, Balanced); Terror all around (Readable)
decisions.reason: The same wording as in 6:25 and 20:3, 10, so the saying can be recognized.

decisions.choice: panic-stricken, falling back; run headlong (Balanced); so afraid, running back; run away fast (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the vision in the present, as the LORD sees it happening, and say "fled in flight" as plain English (m2).

records.source: אַל־יָנ֣וּס הַקַּ֔ל וְאַל־יִמָּלֵ֖ט הַגִּבּ֑וֹר צָפ֨וֹנָה֙ עַל־יַ֣ד נְהַר־פְּרָ֔ת כָּשְׁל֖וּ וְנָפָֽלוּ׃
records.gloss: Let not flee the swift, and let not escape the warrior; northward by [the] side of [the] river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.
pieces: The swift cannot run away, \q the warrior cannot escape. \q In the north, beside the Euphrates River, \q they have stumbled and fallen.

L.6: Let the swift not flee, \q and let the warrior not escape! \q Northward, by the bank of the river Euphrates, \q they have stumbled and fallen.

R.6: Even the fastest runners cannot get away. \q Even the strongest soldiers cannot escape. \q In the north, by the Euphrates River, \q they trip and fall.

decisions.choice: let not flee, let not escape: there will be no escape
decisions.reason: The verbs have the form of a wish or command with "not". Here it states firmly what cannot happen: speed will not save the swift, nor strength the warrior (compare Amos 2:14-15).

decisions.choice: northward by the Euphrates: at Carchemish
decisions.reason: From Judah and Egypt the battlefield lay far to the north, on the upper Euphrates (verse 2). The army that marched so far from home falls there.

decisions.choice: cannot run away ... cannot escape (Balanced); Even ... cannot get away (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the sense of the Hebrew form (m1) rather than giving it as a wish; Readable adds "Even" to bring out that the best soldiers are meant.

records.source: מִי־זֶ֖ה כַּיְאֹ֣ר יַֽעֲלֶ֑ה כַּנְּהָר֕וֹת יִֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ מֵימָֽיו׃
records.gloss: Who [is] this [that] like the Nile rises, like the rivers surge his waters?
pieces: Who is this rising like the Nile, \q like rivers with surging waters?

L.7: Who is this that rises like the Nile, \q whose waters surge like the rivers?

R.7: Who is this, rising like the Nile in flood, \q like rivers whose waters toss and churn?

decisions.choice: the Nile and its rivers: the yearly flood of Egypt's great river
decisions.reason: The word for the Nile is Egyptian in origin. Every year the Nile rose and spread over the land, and in the delta it ran in many branches, the "rivers" of Egypt (Isaiah 7:18; 19:6). The flood was Egypt's life and pride (Ezekiel 29:3, 9).

decisions.choice: who is this: a question answered in the next verse
decisions.reason: The poet asks who is advancing like a flood, as if amazed; verse 8 gives the answer: Egypt. The picture of a nation's army as a flooding river is used of Assyria in Isaiah 8:7-8 and of the Philistines' enemy in 47:2.

decisions.choice: in flood; toss and churn
decisions.reason: Readable adds "in flood" to show that the rising of the river is meant, and gives "surge" as "toss and churn".

records.source: מִצְרַ֨יִם֙ כַּיְאֹ֣ר יַֽעֲלֶ֔ה וְכַנְּהָר֖וֹת יִתְגֹּ֣עֲשׁוּ מָ֑יִם וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אַֽעֲלֶה֙ אֲכַסֶּה־אֶ֔רֶץ אֹבִ֥ידָה עִ֖יר וְיֹ֥שְׁבֵי בָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: Egypt like the Nile rises, and like the rivers surge waters; and it said: I will rise, I will cover [the] earth, I will destroy [the] city and [the] inhabitants in it.
pieces: Egypt rises like the Nile, \q like rivers with surging waters. \q Egypt said, "I will rise and cover the earth; \q I will destroy cities and the people who live in them."

L.8: Egypt rises like the Nile, \q and like the rivers, [its] waters surge. \q And it said, "I will rise, I will cover the earth; \q I will destroy the city and those who live in it."

R.8: It is Egypt that rises like the Nile, \q like rivers whose waters toss and churn. \q Egypt said, "I will rise and cover the whole earth. \q I will destroy cities and the people who live in them."

decisions.choice: it said: Egypt's boast
decisions.reason: The verb is masculine, so the speaker is Egypt as a people or its king, not the city pictured as a woman (verses 11, 19, 24). The army boasts that, like the Nile in flood, it will cover the world. Verses 5-6 have already shown how that boast ends.

decisions.choice: the earth ... the city: the whole world and its cities
decisions.reason: "Earth" here is the whole world, which the flood claims to cover. "City" is singular in Hebrew but stands for every city in the flood's way, and "those who live in it" for their people.

decisions.choice: Egypt said; cities and the people who live in them
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker and make the singular "city" plural, since every city is meant (m2). Readable adds "It is Egypt" to answer the question of verse 7 and "whole" to show the earth is the world.

records.source: עֲל֤וּ הַסּוּסִים֙ וְהִתְהֹלְל֣וּ הָרֶ֔כֶב וְיֵצְא֖וּ הַגִּבּוֹרִ֑ים כּ֤וּשׁ וּפוּט֙ תֹּפְשֵׂ֣י מָגֵ֔ן וְלוּדִ֕ים תֹּפְשֵׂ֖י דֹּ֥רְכֵי קָֽשֶׁת׃
records.gloss: Go up, horses, and drive madly, chariots, and let go out the warriors, Cush and Put, handlers of [the] shield, and Ludites, handlers [and] benders of [the] bow.
pieces: Charge, you horses! Race wildly, you chariots! \q Let the warriors march out, \q Cush and Put, who carry the shield, \q and the Ludites, skilled archers.

L.9: Go up, horses, and drive madly, chariots! \q Let the warriors go out, \q Cush and Put, who handle the shield, \q and the Ludites, who handle and bend the bow.

R.9: Charge, horses! Drive like mad, chariots! \q Let the soldiers march out, \q soldiers from Cush and Put who carry shields, \q and soldiers from Lud who are skilled with bows.

decisions.choice: Cush, Put and the Ludites: African peoples fighting for Egypt
decisions.reason: Cush is the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile, in today's Sudan. Put is a people of Africa, probably in Libya. The Ludites are named among the peoples descended from Egypt (Genesis 10:13), and Lud appears with Put as hired soldiers in Ezekiel 27:10 and 30:5. These are the allies and mercenaries in Egypt's army (verse 21).

decisions.choice: handlers, benders of the bow: skilled archers
decisions.reason: Two participles stand side by side: those who "handle" and those who "tread" the bow. The second describes stringing a bow by stepping on it to bend it (50:14; Isaiah 66:19 has "who draw the bow"). Together they mean expert archers.

decisions.choice: drive madly: race wildly, like madmen
decisions.reason: The verb is the form of "praise" that means to act like one out of one's mind (25:16; 51:7; Nahum 2:5, of chariots racing through the streets).

decisions.choice: the Ludites (Literal, Balanced); soldiers from Lud (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew name is plural, and Genesis 10:13 gives it as "the Ludites". Readable uses the land name Lud, as Isaiah 66:19 has it, and supplies "soldiers from" for each people. Balanced says "skilled archers" for the two participles (m2).

records.source: וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַה֜וּא לַאדֹנָ֧י יְהוִ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת י֤וֹם נְקָמָה֙ לְהִנָּקֵ֣ם מִצָּרָ֔יו וְאָכְלָ֥ה חֶ֨רֶב֙ וְשָׂ֣בְעָ֔ה וְרָוְתָ֖ה מִדָּמָ֑ם כִּ֣י זֶ֠בַח לַאדֹנָ֨י יְהוִ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת בְּאֶ֥רֶץ צָפ֖וֹן אֶל־נְהַר־פְּרָֽת׃
records.gloss: And the day the that [belongs] to [the] Lord Yahweh of hosts, a day of vengeance to avenge himself on his foes; and will devour [the] sword and be satisfied and drink its fill of their blood, for a sacrifice [is] to [the] Lord Yahweh of hosts in [the] land of [the] north by [the] river Euphrates.
pieces: But that day belongs to the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of Armies, a day of vengeance, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} takes vengeance on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies. \q The sword will devour until it is full, \q until it has drunk its fill of their blood. \q For the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of Armies holds a sacrifice in the north country by the Euphrates River.

L.10: But that day [belongs] to the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} foes. \q And the sword will devour and be satisfied \q and drink its fill of their blood. \q For the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of hosts has a sacrifice in the land of the north by the river Euphrates.

R.10: But that day belongs to the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of Armies. It is a day for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to pay back {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies. \q The sword will kill until it is full. \q It will drink their blood until it has had enough. \q The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} of Armies is offering a sacrifice in the land of the north, by the Euphrates River.

decisions.choice: that day belongs to the Lord: the day of battle is his day of vengeance
decisions.reason: The battle at Carchemish is not only Babylon's victory. It is the LORD's day, when he repays his enemies (Isaiah 34:8; 61:2; 63:4; Deuteronomy 32:35, 41-43). Vengeance here is the just repayment of a ruler who puts wrong right, not personal spite.

decisions.choice: the sword will devour and drink its fill: the slaughter will be complete
decisions.reason: The sword is pictured as a creature that eats and drinks until it is full (2:30; 12:12; Deuteronomy 32:42; Isaiah 34:5-6).

decisions.choice: a sacrifice: the fallen army pictured as the LORD's sacrificial feast
decisions.reason: The slain are pictured as animals slaughtered at a sacrifice (Isaiah 34:6; Ezekiel 39:17-19; Zephaniah 1:7-8). Verse 21 continues the picture with the fattened calves.

decisions.choice: the Lord GOD of hosts (Literal); the Lord GOD of Armies (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The set wording of Isaiah and Jeremiah for the Lord with the divine name and "of hosts" (Jeremiah 2:19).

decisions.choice: pay back; kill until it is full
decisions.reason: Readable says "pay back" for taking vengeance (m1) and "kill" for the sword's devouring.

records.source: עֲלִ֤י גִלְעָד֙ וּקְחִ֣י צֳרִ֔י בְּתוּלַ֖ת בַּת־מִצְרָ֑יִם לַשָּׁוְא֙ הִרְבֵּ֣ית רְפֻא֔וֹת תְּעָלָ֖ה אֵ֥ין לָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: Go up [to] Gilead and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt; in vain you have multiplied remedies; new skin there is not for you.
pieces: Go up to Gilead and get balm, \q Virgin Daughter Egypt! \q You have tried remedy after remedy, but in vain; \q there is no healing for you.

L.11: Go up to Gilead and take balm, \q virgin daughter of Egypt! \q In vain you have multiplied remedies; \q there is no new skin for you.

R.11: Go up to Gilead and get healing balm, \q people of Egypt, proud as a young woman! \q But all your medicines are useless. \q Nothing can heal you.

decisions.choice: balm from Gilead: the cure that cannot heal
decisions.reason: Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for a healing resin traded to Egypt (Genesis 37:25). In 8:22 Jeremiah asked whether there was no balm in Gilead for his own people; here Egypt is mockingly told to fetch it, and it will do no good. Babylon is told the same in 51:8.

decisions.choice: virgin daughter of Egypt: the land and its people pictured as a young woman never conquered
decisions.reason: Cities and peoples are pictured as daughters ("daughter Zion"), and "virgin" marks one never yet taken by an enemy (Isaiah 23:12; 47:1). Egypt, proud and untouched, now has a wound that will not heal.

decisions.choice: you have multiplied: the reading aloud, with the same meaning as the written text
alternatives: the written form, with the same sense
decisions.reason: The written text has an older spelling of the ending "you" (to a woman), which the scribes marked to be read in the usual form. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: new skin: the fresh skin that grows over a healing wound
decisions.reason: The word is used in 30:13, "remedies, new skin, there are none for you", of Zion's wound. Egypt's wound, like Zion's, will not close.

decisions.choice: Virgin Daughter Egypt (Balanced); people of Egypt, proud as a young woman (Readable); healing
decisions.reason: Balanced follows Isaiah 47:1, "Virgin Daughter Babylon". Readable says who is addressed and what the picture means (m2). Balanced and Readable say "healing" for new skin, as 30:13 does.

records.source: שָׁמְע֤וּ גוֹיִם֙ קְלוֹנֵ֔ךְ וְצִוְחָתֵ֖ךְ מָלְאָ֣ה הָאָ֑רֶץ כִּֽי־גִבּ֤וֹר בְּגִבּוֹר֙ כָּשָׁ֔לוּ יַחְדָּ֖יו נָפְל֥וּ שְׁנֵיהֶֽם׃פ
records.gloss: Have heard [the] nations your shame, and your outcry has filled the earth; for warrior against warrior they have stumbled, together they have fallen, the two of them.
pieces: The nations have heard of your disgrace; \q the earth is full of your cries. \q One warrior has stumbled over another, \q and both have fallen together.

L.12: The nations have heard of your shame, \q and your outcry has filled the earth; \q for warrior has stumbled against warrior; \q together they have fallen, the two of them.

R.12: The nations have heard how you were shamed. \q Your cries fill the whole earth. \q Your soldiers trip over each other, \q and they all fall down together.

decisions.choice: warrior against warrior: in the rout the soldiers trip over each other
decisions.reason: The picture is of a panicked army running so close together that one man falls over another and both go down (compare Leviticus 26:37). It returns to the stumbling of verse 6.

decisions.choice: your shame ... your outcry: the disgrace of defeat and the cries of the beaten
decisions.reason: Egypt claimed it would cover the earth (verse 8). Now what fills the earth is the sound of its crying, and the nations hear of its humiliation.

decisions.choice: they all fall down together
decisions.reason: Readable makes the pair of fallen warriors stand for the whole army, which is what the picture means (m1).

records.source: הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה אֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הַנָּבִ֑יא לָב֗וֹא נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל לְהַכּ֖וֹת אֶת־אֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: The word that spoke Yahweh to Jeremiah the prophet about [the] coming of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon to strike [the] land of Egypt.
pieces: The word that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon coming to attack the land of Egypt:

L.13: The word that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt:

R.13: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jeremiah the prophet about the time when Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon would come and attack Egypt:

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar's coming to strike Egypt: an attack on Egypt itself, after Carchemish
decisions.reason: The first poem (verses 3-12) is about the battle far away on the Euphrates; this second one (verses 14-24) is about the enemy coming into Egypt. Jeremiah had already acted out such an attack at Tahpanhes (43:8-13). A broken Babylonian chronicle tablet is usually taken to record a campaign of Nebuchadrezzar against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568 BC; this is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: a new heading
decisions.reason: The heading has a different form from verse 1 ("the word that the LORD spoke", compare 50:1). It marks the start of a second oracle about Egypt. The name has the form Nebuchadrezzar, as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: about the time when ... would come and attack
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the message looks ahead to an attack still to come.

records.heading: Egypt will be struck

records.source: הַגִּ֤ידוּ בְמִצְרַ֨יִם֙ וְהַשְׁמִ֣יעוּ בְמִגְדּ֔וֹל וְהַשְׁמִ֥יעוּ בְנֹ֖ף וּבְתַחְפַּנְחֵ֑ס אִמְר֗וּ הִתְיַצֵּב֙ וְהָכֵ֣ן לָ֔ךְ כִּֽי־אָכְלָ֥ה חֶ֖רֶב סְבִיבֶֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol, and proclaim in Noph and in Tahpanhes; say: Take your stand and prepare yourself, for has devoured [the] sword [those] around you.
pieces: Announce it in Egypt, proclaim it in Migdol, \q proclaim it in Memphis and in Tahpanhes. \q Say, "Take your position and make ready, \q for the sword is devouring all around you."

L.14: Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; \q proclaim in Memphis and in Tahpanhes. \q Say, "Take your stand and get yourself ready, \q for the sword has devoured those around you."

R.14: Announce this in Egypt. Spread the news in the towns of Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes. \q Tell them, "Get into position and be ready to fight! \q War is destroying everyone around you."

decisions.choice: Migdol, Noph and Tahpanhes: cities of northern Egypt
decisions.reason: Migdol was a fortress on Egypt's north-eastern border and Tahpanhes a frontier city in the eastern delta; Noph is Memphis, the old capital near the head of the delta (2:16; Isaiah 19:13). Judeans who fled to Egypt had settled in all three (43:7; 44:1). An enemy from Asia would reach them first.

decisions.choice: the sword has devoured those around you: the neighbors have already fallen
decisions.reason: The verb is past: the sword has already eaten up Egypt's neighbors, and Egypt is next. The commands to take position are given to Egypt as a single soldier ("you" is singular).

decisions.choice: Memphis
decisions.reason: All levels use the familiar name Memphis for Noph, as in 2:16 and Isaiah 19:13.

decisions.choice: War is destroying
decisions.reason: Readable says "war" for the sword, as the book's set phrase does ("war, famine and disease").

records.source: מַדּ֖וּעַ נִסְחַ֣ף אַבִּירֶ֑יךָ לֹ֣א עָמַ֔ד כִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה הֲדָפֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Why has been swept away your mighty one? Not he stood, for Yahweh thrust him down.
pieces: Why is your mighty one swept away? \q He could not stand, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} drove him down.

L.15: Why has your mighty one been swept away? \q He did not stand, \q because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} thrust him down.

R.15: Egypt, why has your strong one been swept away? \q He could not stand his ground, \q because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pushed him down.

decisions.choice: why has your mighty one been swept away (Hebrew)
alternatives: Why has Apis fled? Your chosen calf did not stand
decisions.reason: The Greek translation reads the Hebrew letters differently, dividing the verb into two words: "Why has Apis fled? Your chosen calf did not stand." Apis was the sacred bull worshiped at Memphis (verse 14). If that reading is right, the verse mocks Egypt's bull-god, unable to stand before the LORD. The Hebrew, which is followed here, speaks of a "mighty one" without naming him. This is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: your mighty one: a strong man, a bull, or Egypt's champion
decisions.reason: The word means "strong one". It is used of warriors (Lamentations 1:15), of powerful bulls (Psalm 22:13; 50:13), and in a related form of God as "the Mighty One of Jacob". Here it may be Egypt's god (the bull Apis), its king, or its strongest troops. The Hebrew form is plural, "your mighty ones", but the verbs that follow are singular, and some Hebrew manuscripts have the singular; the singular is followed.

decisions.choice: the LORD thrust him down
decisions.reason: The rout has a cause beyond the enemy: the LORD himself pushed Egypt's champion over, as one pushes a man off his feet.

decisions.choice: Egypt, ... strong one ... stand his ground
decisions.reason: Readable names who is addressed and keeps the open word "strong one" (m2) so that it can mean a god, a king or a warrior.

records.source: הִרְבָּ֖ה כּוֹשֵׁ֑ל גַּם־נָפַ֞ל אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֗הוּ וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ ק֣וּמָה׀וְנָשֻׁ֣בָה אֶל־עַמֵּ֗נוּ וְאֶל־אֶ֨רֶץ֙ מֽוֹלַדְתֵּ֔נוּ מִפְּנֵ֖י חֶ֥רֶב הַיּוֹנָֽה׃
records.gloss: He has multiplied [the] stumbler; also he has fallen, each to his neighbor, and they said: Arise, and let us return to our people and to [the] land of our birth, from before [the] sword of the oppressor.
pieces: He made many stumble; \q they fell over one another. And they said, "Up! Let us go back to our own people and to the land where we were born, \q away from the oppressor's sword!"

L.16: He made many stumble; \q indeed, they fell, each against his neighbor, and they said, "Get up, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, \q away from the oppressor's sword!"

R.16: He made many soldiers trip. \q They fell over one another. They said, "Get up! Let us go home to our own people, to the land where we were born, \q to get away from the enemy's cruel sword!"

decisions.choice: he multiplied the stumbler: he made many stumble
decisions.reason: The verb "make many" has the LORD of verse 15 as its subject, and "the one stumbling" stands for every soldier who trips. The stumbling of verses 6 and 12 spreads through the army.

decisions.choice: let us go back to our own people: the foreign soldiers give up
decisions.reason: Those who speak have a people and a homeland elsewhere. They are most likely the hired troops of verses 9 and 21, who leave Egypt to its fate (compare the same words in 50:16, of foreigners in Babylon).

decisions.choice: the oppressor's sword: the sword of the cruel enemy
decisions.reason: The word is a participle, "oppressing", from a verb used of treating people with violence (22:3). The same phrase is used in 50:16 and, of the destroyer, in 25:38. It has the same letters as the word for "dove", but "oppressor" fits every place it is used.

decisions.choice: soldiers; the enemy's cruel sword
decisions.reason: Readable supplies who stumbles and says who the oppressor is.

records.source: קָרְא֖וּ שָׁ֑ם פַּרְעֹ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֨יִם֙ שָׁא֔וֹן הֶעֱבִ֖יר הַמּוֹעֵֽד׃
records.gloss: They called there: Pharaoh king of Egypt [is] a noise; he has let pass the appointed time.
pieces: There they cried out, \q "Pharaoh king of Egypt is only a loud noise; \q he has let his moment pass."

L.17: They called out there, \q "Pharaoh king of Egypt [is but] a noise; \q he has let the appointed time pass by."

R.17: There they say, \q "Pharaoh king of Egypt is just a lot of noise. \q He missed his chance."

decisions.choice: a noise who let the appointed time pass: a mocking nickname for Pharaoh
alternatives: They called Pharaoh king of Egypt 'Noise, who let the appointed time pass'
decisions.reason: "Called" can mean "gave a name", as in 20:3, and the words that follow sound like a nickname: "Loud Noise, who let the appointed time go by". Pharaoh made a great din of threats and promises but missed his moment to act, as Isaiah called Egypt "Rahab who sits still" (Isaiah 30:7). The Greek translation reads "call the name of Pharaoh Neco", treating the words as a name; this is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: noise: the roar of a crowd or an army, a loud din
decisions.reason: The word is used of the roar of armies and of rushing waters (25:31; 48:45; Isaiah 17:12-13). Egypt, which rose roaring like the Nile (verses 7-8), turns out to be only sound.

decisions.choice: they called there: the soldiers who flee
decisions.reason: "They" are most likely the soldiers of verse 16, who shout this as they leave; "there" is the place of the defeat.

decisions.choice: [is but] a noise (Literal); only a loud noise (Balanced); just a lot of noise (Readable); let his moment pass / missed his chance
decisions.reason: Each level keeps the words as a saying about Pharaoh and gives "let the appointed time pass" in plain English at Balanced and Readable. The footnote gives the reading as a nickname (m1).

records.source: חַי־אָ֨נִי֙ נְאֻם־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁמ֑וֹ כִּ֚י כְּתָב֣וֹר בֶּֽהָרִ֔ים וּכְכַרְמֶ֖ל בַּיָּ֥ם יָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: [As] I live, declares the King, Yahweh of hosts [is] his name, surely like Tabor among the mountains, and like Carmel by the sea, he will come.
pieces: As I live, declares the King, \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies is {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name, \q one is coming who is like Tabor among the mountains, \q like Carmel by the sea.

L.18: As I live, declares the King, \q whose name [is] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, \q surely like Tabor among the mountains \q and like Carmel by the sea, he will come.

R.18: As surely as I live, says the King, \q whose name is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, \q someone is coming who towers like Mount Tabor over the mountains \q and like Mount Carmel over the sea.

decisions.choice: as I live: an oath
decisions.reason: God swears by his own life, the most solemn oath there is (22:24; Numbers 14:21; Isaiah 49:18). What follows is certain.

decisions.choice: Tabor and Carmel: mountains that stand out above everything around them
decisions.reason: Mount Tabor rises alone out of the plain of Jezreel, and the ridge of Carmel stands high above the Mediterranean coast. The one who is coming stands out above every power in the same way.

decisions.choice: he will come: the conqueror, unnamed here
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. The heading (verse 13) shows that it is Nebuchadrezzar, the one "coming" against Egypt; verses 20 and 24 speak of him as coming from the north.

decisions.choice: the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts
decisions.reason: Pharaoh is "king of Egypt" (verse 17), but the true King is the LORD (10:7, 10). The same title returns in 48:15 and 51:57.

decisions.choice: one is coming (Balanced); someone is coming who towers ... Mount (Readable); As surely as I live (Readable); the LORD of Armies is his name (Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable words the oath "As surely as I live", the usual English form of this oath, and Balanced keeps the Hebrew order of the title, "the LORD of Armies is his name". Both also supply a subject for "he will come" (m3), and Readable adds "Mount" and "towers" to show what the comparison means (m2).

records.source: כְּלֵ֤י גוֹלָה֙ עֲשִׂ֣י לָ֔ךְ יוֹשֶׁ֖בֶת בַּת־מִצְרָ֑יִם כִּֽי־נֹף֙ לְשַׁמָּ֣ה תִֽהְיֶ֔ה וְנִצְּתָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ין יוֹשֵֽׁב׃ס
records.gloss: Baggage of exile make for yourself, dweller daughter of Egypt; for Noph will become a waste and be laid in ruins, without inhabitant.
pieces: Pack your bags for exile, \q you people of Daughter Egypt! \q For Memphis will become a wasteland, \q a ruin where no one lives.

L.19: Make yourself baggage for exile, \q you who dwell [there], daughter of Egypt! \q For Memphis will become a waste, \q and it will be laid in ruins, without inhabitant.

R.19: People of Egypt, \q pack your bags to be taken away as prisoners! \q The city of Memphis will become an empty ruin. \q No one will live there.

decisions.choice: baggage of exile: the few things a captive could carry
decisions.reason: People taken into exile walked with a small bundle on their shoulders (Ezekiel 12:3-7). Egypt, which hoped to cover the earth, is told to get ready to be led away.

decisions.choice: dweller daughter of Egypt: the people of Egypt, pictured as a woman
decisions.reason: The two words are joined: the one who lives as Daughter Egypt, that is, the people of the land pictured as a woman (verses 11, 24; compare 48:18, "dweller daughter of Dibon").

decisions.choice: be laid in ruins: be destroyed so that nothing stands
decisions.reason: The verb is used of cities laid waste (2:15; 4:7). Memphis, the old royal city (verse 14), will be left without people.

decisions.choice: you people of Daughter Egypt (Balanced); People of Egypt ... to be taken away as prisoners (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom the words address (m2); Readable explains exile and adds "the city of".

records.source: עֶגְלָ֥ה יְפֵֽה־פִיָּ֖ה מִצְרָ֑יִם קֶ֥רֶץ מִצָּפ֖וֹן בָּ֥א בָֽא׃
records.gloss: A heifer very beautiful [is] Egypt; a gadfly from [the] north has come, has come.
pieces: Egypt is a lovely young heifer, \q but a gadfly from the north is coming, coming on!

L.20: A very beautiful heifer [is] Egypt; \q a gadfly from the north has come, has come!

R.20: Egypt is like a beautiful young cow. \q But a stinging fly from the north is coming to attack her!

decisions.choice: gadfly: a biting fly that torments cattle
decisions.reason: The word is found only here. It comes from a root meaning "to nip" or "pinch", and in a herd picture it most likely means a biting fly such as a gadfly or horsefly, which drives cattle wild. Others understand it as "destruction" or "one who cuts off". Either way, the enemy from the north attacks the sleek heifer.

decisions.choice: a very beautiful heifer: Egypt, sleek and well fed
decisions.reason: The rare doubled word means "very pretty". A young cow fattened in good pasture pictures a rich, untroubled land (compare Hosea 10:11; Amos 4:1). It may also glance at Egypt's honor for sacred cattle (verse 15).

decisions.choice: has come, has come: the Hebrew repeats the verb
decisions.reason: The doubled verb gives urgency: it is coming, it is here. Many Hebrew manuscripts and some ancient translations read the second word with one more letter, "has come against her". The meaning is close. This is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: lovely young heifer; coming, coming on (Balanced); like a beautiful young cow; stinging fly ... to attack her (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the doubled verb as "coming, coming on". Readable makes the picture a comparison, says "stinging fly" for gadfly (m1), and says what the fly will do.

records.source: גַּם־שְׂכִרֶ֤יהָ בְקִרְבָּהּ֙ כְּעֶגְלֵ֣י מַרְבֵּ֔ק כִּֽי־גַם־הֵ֧מָּה הִפְנ֛וּ נָ֥סוּ יַחְדָּ֖יו לֹ֣א עָמָ֑דוּ כִּ֣י י֥וֹם אֵידָ֛ם בָּ֥א עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם עֵ֥ת פְּקֻדָּתָֽם׃
records.gloss: Also her hired [soldiers] in her midst [are] like calves of [the] stall; for also they have turned, they have fled together, not they stood; for [the] day of their calamity has come upon them, [the] time of their punishment.
pieces: Even the hired soldiers in her ranks are like fattened calves; \q they too have turned and fled together, they did not stand their ground; \q for the day of their disaster has come upon them, the time of their punishment.

L.21: Even her hired soldiers in her midst [are] like calves of the stall; \q for they too have turned, they have fled together, they did not stand; \q for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment.

R.21: Even the soldiers Egypt hired are like fat calves ready to be killed. \q They too turn and run away together. They do not stand and fight. \q The day of their disaster has come. It is time for them to be punished.

decisions.choice: hired soldiers: the foreign mercenaries in Egypt's army
decisions.reason: Egypt's army in this period relied heavily on hired troops from other lands, such as those named in verse 9. They are the ones who say "let us go back to our own people" in verse 16.

decisions.choice: calves of the stall: animals fattened for slaughter
decisions.reason: Calves kept in the stall were fed up to be killed for a feast (Amos 6:4; 1 Samuel 28:24). The well-paid soldiers are ready for the LORD's "sacrifice" (verse 10).

decisions.choice: the time of their punishment: the time when God calls them to account
decisions.reason: The noun is from the verb "to visit", used of God coming to deal with someone, here in judgment (8:12; 10:15; 11:23).

decisions.choice: fat calves ready to be killed
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the fattened calves picture (m2).

records.source: קוֹלָ֖הּ כַּנָּחָ֣שׁ יֵלֵ֑ךְ כִּֽי־בְחַ֣יִל יֵלֵ֔כוּ וּבְקַרְדֻּמּוֹת֙ בָּ֣אוּ לָ֔הּ כְּחֹטְבֵ֖י עֵצִֽים׃
records.gloss: Her sound like a snake [that] goes, for in strength they go, and with axes they come to her, like cutters of trees.
pieces: She makes a sound like a snake slithering away, \q as her enemies march in force \q and come at her with axes, \q like woodcutters felling trees.

L.22: Her sound is like a snake that goes away, \q for they march in force \q and come against her with axes, \q like those who cut down trees.

R.22: Egypt hisses like a snake as it slides away, \q because her enemies are coming with a strong army. \q They come at her with axes, \q like woodcutters cutting down trees.

decisions.choice: her sound like a snake that goes: the faint hiss of a snake escaping
decisions.reason: Egypt rose roaring like the Nile (verses 7-8) and Pharaoh was a "noise" (verse 17). Now all that is heard is the rustle and hiss of a snake slipping away through the undergrowth as the woodcutters come.

decisions.choice: they: the invaders from the north
decisions.reason: "They" are not named; they are the enemy of verses 20 and 24, the people of the north.

decisions.choice: with axes, like woodcutters: the army pictured as felling a forest
decisions.reason: The picture continues into verse 23: the invaders cut down Egypt like trees (compare 22:7; Isaiah 10:33-34, of Assyria).

decisions.choice: slithering away (Balanced); hisses ... slides away (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of sound and movement the picture means (m1); Readable supplies "hisses" and names Egypt.

records.source: כָּרְת֤וּ יַעְרָהּ֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֖י לֹ֣א יֵֽחָקֵ֑ר כִּ֤י רַבּוּ֙ מֵֽאַרְבֶּ֔ה וְאֵ֥ין לָהֶ֖ם מִסְפָּֽר׃
records.gloss: They have cut down her forest, declares Yahweh, though not it can be searched; for they are more numerous than locusts, and there is not to them number.
pieces: They will cut down her forest, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q dense as it is, \q for they are more than locusts; \q they cannot be counted.

L.23: They have cut down her forest, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q though it cannot be searched out; \q for they are more numerous than locusts, \q and there is no number to them.

R.23: They will cut down her forest, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q even though it is too thick to walk through. \q The enemy soldiers are more than a swarm of locusts. \q No one can count them.

decisions.choice: though it cannot be searched out: a forest too dense to go through
alternatives: for they cannot be searched out (counted)
decisions.reason: The verb means to search or explore (Job 5:9, of things beyond searching). The forest is so thick that no one can make their way into it, yet the invaders cut it down. The clause could instead be read with what follows, "for they cannot be counted", but that is said in the last line.

decisions.choice: her forest: Egypt's people and strength pictured as trees
decisions.reason: A forest stands for a nation's multitude and pride (21:14; Isaiah 10:18-19).

decisions.choice: more than locusts: a vast army
decisions.reason: Locust swarms were the picture of numbers beyond counting (Judges 6:5; 7:12; Nahum 3:15).

decisions.choice: will cut down
decisions.reason: The verb is past in form, describing the coming judgment as if done. Balanced and Readable put it in the future, which is what it means here; Readable adds "the enemy soldiers" for "they".

records.source: הֹבִ֖ישָׁה בַּת־מִצְרָ֑יִם נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּיַ֥ד עַם־צָפֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: Is put to shame [the] daughter of Egypt; she has been given into [the] hand of [the] people of [the] north.
pieces: Daughter Egypt is put to shame, \q handed over to the people of the north.

L.24: The daughter of Egypt has been put to shame; \q she has been given into the hand of the people of the north.

R.24: The people of Egypt will be disgraced. \q They will be handed over to the people from the north.

decisions.choice: daughter of Egypt: Egypt pictured as a woman
decisions.reason: As in verses 11 and 19. The poem ends with the proud young woman shamed and handed over.

decisions.choice: the people of the north: Babylon
decisions.reason: From his call Jeremiah spoke of a disaster coming from the north (1:14-15; 6:22). The heading at verse 13 shows that it is Babylon under Nebuchadrezzar; it now falls on Egypt as it fell on Judah.

decisions.choice: will be disgraced ... will be handed over
decisions.reason: Readable puts the past-tense verbs into the future, which is what the prophecy means, and names the people for "daughter".

records.gloss: Says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel: Behold I [am] punishing Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, and her gods, and her kings, and Pharaoh, and those trusting in him.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: I am about to punish Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh, and Egypt with her gods and her kings, Pharaoh and all who trust in him.

L.25: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel, says: See, I am about to punish Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, and her gods, and her kings, and Pharaoh and those who trust in him.

R.25: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: I am going to punish Amon, the god of Thebes. I will punish Pharaoh and Egypt, with her gods and her kings. I will punish Pharaoh and everyone who trusts in him.

decisions.choice: Amon of No: Amon, the god of Thebes
decisions.reason: No is the Hebrew name of Thebes, the great city of Upper Egypt (Ezekiel 30:14-16; Nahum 3:8, "No-amon"). Amon was its chief god, worshiped as king of the gods. The judgment begins with the god on whom Egypt relied.

decisions.choice: punishing her gods: the LORD judges the gods of Egypt
decisions.reason: As at the exodus (Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4) and in Jeremiah's sign at Tahpanhes (43:12-13), the LORD's judgment falls on Egypt's gods as well as on its people. The verb is "visit", used of calling to account (verse 21).

decisions.choice: Pharaoh named twice: the stress falls on those who trust in him
decisions.reason: Pharaoh is named in the list and again at the end with "those who trust in him". These include Judeans who looked to Egypt for safety instead of to the LORD (2:36-37; 37:7; 42:13-17; Isaiah 30:1-3; 31:1).

decisions.choice: Thebes
decisions.reason: All levels give No its familiar name Thebes, as Memphis is given for Noph (verse 14). A footnote can give the Hebrew name.

decisions.choice: See, I am about to punish
decisions.reason: The Hebrew opens God's words with a call to attention and a participle of what is about to happen; the wording follows 20:4. Readable repeats "I will punish" to keep the long list clear.

records.source: וּנְתַתִּ֗ים בְּיַד֙ מְבַקְשֵׁ֣י נַפְשָׁ֔ם וּבְיַ֛ד נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֥ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל וּבְיַד־עֲבָדָ֑יו וְאַחֲרֵי־כֵ֛ן תִּשְׁכֹּ֥ן כִּֽימֵי־קֶ֖דֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And I will give them into [the] hand of [those] seeking their life, and into [the] hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into [the] hand of his servants; and after this she will dwell as [in the] days of old, declares Yahweh.
pieces: I will hand them over to those who want to kill them, to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and his officials. But afterward Egypt will be lived in again as in former days, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.26: And I will give them into the hand of those who seek their life, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants. But afterward she will be inhabited as in the days of old, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.26: I will hand them over to the people who want to kill them. I will hand them over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and his officials. But later, people will live in Egypt again as they did long ago, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: those who seek their life: those who want to kill them
decisions.reason: "Seek someone's life" means to try to kill (4:30; 11:21; 19:7).

decisions.choice: afterward she will be inhabited as in the days of old: Egypt will recover
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine, so its subject is Egypt pictured as a woman. After the judgment the land will be lived in again. Jeremiah gives similar promises for Moab, Ammon and Elam (48:47; 49:6, 39); compare Isaiah 19:22-25 and Ezekiel 29:13-14.

decisions.choice: verse 26 kept, as the Hebrew text has it
alternatives: omit the verse with the Greek
decisions.reason: The Greek translation of Jeremiah does not have this verse. The Hebrew text, which this translation follows, has it. This is written from general knowledge (see 1:1).

decisions.choice: his officials
decisions.reason: "Servants" of a king are his court officials, so Balanced and Readable say "officials", as Isaiah does. The name keeps the form Nebuchadrezzar, as in verses 2 and 13.

decisions.choice: Egypt will be lived in again (Balanced); people will live in Egypt again (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Egypt as the subject (m2) and say plainly that "dwell" here means being inhabited.

records.source: וְ֠אַתָּה אַל־תִּירָ֞א עַבְדִּ֤י יַֽעֲקֹב֙ וְאַל־תֵּחַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּ֠י הִנְנִ֤י מוֹשִֽׁעֲךָ֙ מֵֽרָח֔וֹק וְאֶֽת־זַרְעֲךָ֖ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ שִׁבְיָ֑ם וְשָׁ֧ב יַעֲק֛וֹב וְשָׁקַ֥ט וְשַׁאֲנַ֖ן וְאֵ֥ין מַחֲרִֽיד׃ס
records.gloss: And you, do not fear, my servant Jacob, and do not be dismayed, Israel; for look, I [am] saving you from afar, and your offspring from [the] land of their captivity; and Jacob will return and be quiet and be at ease, and there [will be] none making [him] afraid.
pieces: But you, Jacob {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant, do not be afraid; do not be dismayed, Israel. \q For I will save you from a far country, and your descendants from the land where they are captives. \q Jacob will come home and have quiet and rest, and no one will make him afraid.

L.27: And you, do not fear, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant Jacob, and do not be dismayed, Israel, \q for look, I am saving you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. \q And Jacob will return and be quiet and at ease, and there will be no one to make [him] afraid.

R.27: But do not be afraid, Jacob, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant. Israel, do not be frightened. \q I will save you from a land far away. I will save your children from the land where they are prisoners. \q The people of Jacob will come home. They will live in peace and safety, and no one will frighten them.

decisions.choice: do not fear, my servant Jacob: the words of 30:10, repeated here
decisions.reason: Verses 27-28 repeat 30:10-11 almost word for word, and the wording here follows those verses. Verse 27 differs in one point: 30:10 has "declares the LORD" after "my servant Jacob", and here it is missing (it comes in verse 28). After the oracle against Egypt, the promise turns to Israel: the nation it trusted will fall, but God's people will come home.

decisions.choice: my servant: Israel as the people the LORD has chosen and keeps
decisions.reason: As in 30:10. It is a title of honor, not of bondage (Isaiah 41:8-9; 44:1-2).

decisions.choice: I am saving you from far away: a sure promise, spoken as if already under way
decisions.reason: As in 30:10.

decisions.choice: the wording of 30:10
decisions.reason: The levels keep the wording of 30:10 so that a reader hears the same promise in both places, leaving out only "declares the LORD" (m1). Balanced and Readable begin "But" rather than the "So" of 30:10, because here the promise is set against Egypt's fate.

decisions.choice: The people of Jacob ... They ... them
decisions.reason: As in 30:10.

records.heading: Comfort for Jacob

records.source: אַ֠תָּה אַל־תִּירָ֞א עַבְדִּ֤י יַֽעֲקֹב֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֥י אִתְּךָ֖ אָ֑נִי כִּי֩ אֶעֱשֶׂ֨ה כָלָ֜ה בְּכָֽל־הַגּוֹיִ֣ם׀אֲשֶׁ֧ר הִדַּחְתִּ֣יךָ שָׁ֗מָּה וְאֹֽתְךָ֙ לֹא־אֶעֱשֶׂ֣ה כָלָ֔ה וְיִסַּרְתִּ֨יךָ֙ לַמִּשְׁפָּ֔ט וְנַקֵּ֖ה לֹ֥א אֲנַקֶּֽךָּ׃ס
records.gloss: You, do not fear, my servant Jacob, declares Yahweh, for with you I [am]; for I will make [a] full end of all the nations where I have driven you there, but you I will not make [a] full end [of]; and I will discipline you in justice, and leaving unpunished I will not leave you unpunished.
pieces: You, Jacob {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant, do not be afraid, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, because I am with you. \q I will bring to an end all the nations among whom I drove you, but you I will not bring to an end. \q I will discipline you, but justly, \q and I will not let you go unpunished.

L.28: You, do not fear, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant Jacob, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for I [am] with you. \q For I will make a full end of all the nations where I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. \q I will discipline you in just measure, \q and I will by no means leave you unpunished.

R.28: Do not be afraid, Jacob, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I am with you. \q I will completely destroy all the nations where I drove you. But I will not completely destroy you. \q I will correct you, but I will be fair, \q and I will not let you escape all punishment.

decisions.choice: the words of 30:11, with three differences
decisions.reason: The verse follows 30:11 closely. It differs in three places. It opens by repeating "do not fear, my servant Jacob" with "declares the LORD", which here moves from verse 27. It says "for I am with you" without the words "to save you" that follow in 30:11. And it says "where I have driven you" where 30:11 has "where I have scattered you". It also joins "but you I will not make a full end" with a plain "and" where 30:11 has a stronger "only". The promise is the same.

decisions.choice: a full end: complete destruction
decisions.reason: As in 30:11.

decisions.choice: discipline you in justice: correct you in fair measure, not to destroy you
decisions.reason: As in 30:11 (compare 10:24).

decisions.choice: leaving unpunished I will not leave you unpunished: I will certainly not let you go free of punishment
decisions.reason: As in 30:11.

decisions.choice: the wording of 30:11; driven (Literal); drove (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The levels keep the wording of 30:11 wherever the Hebrew is the same, and change only where it differs (m1): the repeated opening, "I am with you" on its own, and "driven" or "drove" for "scattered".

decisions.choice: I will correct you, but I will be fair
decisions.reason: As in 30:11.
